subject: Physics
title: Wave Optics
summary: Wave optics treats light as a wave to explain what ray optics cannot: interference, diffraction and polarisation. By Huygens' principle every point of a wavefront acts as a new source; the secondary wavelets combine to form the next wavefront — this also gives the laws of reflection and refraction.

When waves from two coherent sources (same frequency, constant phase difference) overlap, bright (constructive) and dark (destructive) fringes appear — interference. In Young's double slit, fringe width β = λD/d.
Light also bends slightly at a single slit and forms a pattern — diffraction. The central bright fringe is the widest and brightest (width 2λD/a); the first dark fringe is at a sin θ = λ.

Light is a transverse wave, so it can be polarised. A Polaroid passes vibrations in only one direction; between two Polaroids Malus' law I = I₀ cos²θ holds. Reflection also polarises light — at the Brewster angle the reflected light is completely polarised.

formulas.name: Path difference and phase difference
formulas.when: Condition at a point in interference.
formulas.note: Use the wavelength in the medium where the path lies (λ/n).

formulas.name: Resultant intensity of two waves
formulas.formula: I = I₁ + I₂ + 2√(I₁I₂) cos φ;   equal: I = 4I₀ cos²(φ/2)
formulas.note: For incoherent sources it is just I₁ + I₂ — no cosine term.

formulas.name: Maxima and minima intensities
formulas.note: If an amplitude ratio is given, square it first — it isn't the intensity ratio.

formulas.name: Constructive and destructive conditions
formulas.when: Whether a point is bright or dark.

formulas.name: YDSE fringe width and positions
formulas.formula: β = λD/d;   nth bright: y = nλD/d;   nth dark: y = (2n − 1)λD/2d;   angular width = λ/d
formulas.mistake: Don't mix D and d: D is the screen distance (large), d the slit separation (small).

formulas.name: Thin film in front of one slit
formulas.when: Glass sheet in front of one slit.
formulas.note: The pattern shifts towards the slit with the sheet; fringe width doesn't change.

formulas.name: Single-slit diffraction
formulas.formula: Minima: a sin θ = nλ;   central max angular width = 2λ/a;   linear width = 2λD/a
formulas.mistake: Opposite of YDSE: here a sin θ = nλ gives DARK, not bright.

formulas.name: Huygens: refraction
formulas.formula: sin i / sin r = v₁/v₂ = n₂/n₁;   λ₂ = λ₁ v₂/v₁;   f same
formulas.mistake: Frequency never changes from one medium to another.

formulas.name: Brewster's law
formulas.formula: tan θ_B = n;   θ_B + r = 90° (reflected ⊥ refracted)
formulas.note: At Brewster's angle the reflected light is fully polarised, the refracted light only partly.

formulas.name: Malus' law
formulas.formula: I = I₀ cos²θ;   unpolarised light through a Polaroid: I₀/2
formulas.note: Unpolarised light is halved at the first Polaroid — apply cos² after that.

formulas.name: Coherent sources
formulas.formula: Same frequency + constant phase difference;   YDSE / Lloyd's mirror / biprism make two from one source
formulas.mistake: Two separate bulbs are never coherent — the pattern changes instantly.

examples.title: YDSE numbers
examples.problem: λ = 600 nm, d = 0.5 mm, D = 1 m. Fringe width, third bright and third dark fringe?
examples.solution: β = λD/d = 600 × 10⁻⁹ × 1 / 0.5 × 10⁻³ = 1.2 mm. 3rd bright = 3β = 3.6 mm. 3rd dark = 2.5β = 3 mm.

examples.title: Set-up in water
examples.problem: The set-up above is immersed in water (n = 4/3). New fringe width?

examples.title: Intensity ratio
examples.problem: Two coherent sources have intensities I and 4I. I_max : I_min?

examples.title: Intensity from path difference
examples.problem: Two equal sources (I₀ each), λ = 600 nm, path difference 150 nm at a point. Intensity?
examples.solution: φ = 2π × 150/600 = π/2. I = 4I₀ cos²(π/4) = 2I₀ (half the maximum).

examples.title: Single slit
examples.problem: a = 0.2 mm, λ = 500 nm, screen at D = 2 m. Angle of the first minimum and width of the central maximum?

examples.title: Brewster angle
examples.problem: Brewster angle for glass with n = √3, and the angle of refraction then?

examples.title: Two Polaroids
examples.problem: Unpolarised light I₀ passes through two Polaroids whose axes are at 60°. Final intensity?
examples.solution: After the first: I₀/2. After the second: (I₀/2)cos²60° = (I₀/2)(1/4) = 0.125I₀ (12.5%).

examples.title: Fringe shift from a glass sheet
examples.problem: In YDSE a 6 μm glass sheet (n = 1.5) covers one slit, λ = 600 nm. How many fringes shift?
examples.solution: N = (n − 1)t/λ = 0.5 × 6 × 10⁻⁶ / 600 × 10⁻⁹ = 5 fringes, towards the covered slit.

examples.title: Light in glass
examples.problem: Light of 600 nm (in air) enters glass (n = 1.5). Speed, wavelength, frequency?
examples.solution: v = c/n = 2.0 × 10⁸ m/s. λ = 600/1.5 = 400 nm. f = c/λ_air = 5.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz — same in both media.

topics.title: Wavefront and Huygens' principle
topics.explain: A wavefront is a surface of points in the same phase (spherical from a point source, plane far away). Huygens: every point on a wavefront sends out secondary wavelets; the surface touching them all is the new wavefront. Rays are always perpendicular to wavefronts.

topics.title: Reflection and refraction from Huygens' principle
topics.explain: When a plane wavefront meets a surface obliquely, each point sends a wavelet. In the same medium wavelets travel at the same speed ⇒ i = r (reflection). In the second medium the speed is v₂ ⇒ sin i/sin r = v₁/v₂ (Snell's law). This showed that light is slower in a denser medium (Newton's corpuscular theory predicted the opposite).

topics.title: Coherent sources and sustained interference
topics.explain: For a steady pattern the sources must be coherent (same f, constant phase), with nearly equal amplitudes, and the slits narrow and close. Two separate bulbs are not coherent — their phase changes randomly every ~10⁻⁸ s.

topics.title: Young's double slit experiment
topics.explain: Light from one source passes through two narrow slits, giving two coherent sources. The screen shows equally wide bright and dark fringes with a bright centre. White light gives a white centre and coloured fringes. Energy is not destroyed — only redistributed.

topics.title: Diffraction due to a single slit
topics.explain: Each part of the slit sends wavelets; at θ where the two halves of the slit differ in path by λ/2, everything cancels ⇒ first dark fringe at a sin θ = λ. The central maximum is twice as wide as the others. A narrower slit spreads the pattern more.

topics.title: Interference vs diffraction
topics.explain: Interference: two (or more) separate wavefronts, all fringes equally wide and about equally bright. Diffraction: parts of a single wavefront, central fringe widest and brightest, the rest fading gradually.

topics.title: Polarisation and its uses
topics.explain: Light is transverse — its vibrations can be restricted to one plane. Polarisation by Polaroids, reflection (Brewster) and scattering (skylight is partly polarised). Uses: sunglasses (reduce glare), 3D movie glasses, LCD screens, stress analysis, camera filters.
